papers.title: MusicRWKV: A Multimodal RWKV Framework for Music Representation Learning
papers.abstract: Recent music foundation models have achieved remarkable progress in music representation learning, yet most existing approaches rely on Transformer architectures whose quadratic attention complexity introduces substantial computational and memory overhead when modeling long-duration music recordings. In this work, we propose MusicRWKV, a multimodal music representation learning framework built upon the RWKV architecture. MusicRWKV jointly models waveform, spectrogram, and metadata information within a unified self-supervised learning framework. To improve efficiency for long musical sequences, we introduce an invertible compression module that reduces sequence length while preserving reconstruction capability. A FiLM-based conditioning strategy is employed to facilitate modality-aware representation learning without introducing expensive cross-attention operations. We further investigate the integration of Soft ROSA as a differentiable retrieval mechanism for neural-symbolic interaction. Experimental evaluation across a diverse collection of Music Information Retrieval (MIR) benchmarks demonstrates that the proposed RWKV-based architecture can be effectively adapted to heterogeneous music understanding tasks. A controlled pretraining ablation shows that Soft ROSA improves validation performance, while layer-wise telemetry analysis reveals a progressive transition from distributed retrieval to selective retrieval in deeper network layers. These results suggest that RWKV provides a promising architectural alternative to Transformer-based models for multimodal music understanding.
reasons: Music Foundation Models & Representations: music foundation model, music representation learning, music understanding

papers.title: Harmony: Bridging Audio Understanding and Editing through Agentic Collaboration
papers.abstract: Natural-language audio editing requires connecting a user's intent to specific sounds and time regions while preserving surrounding content. Complex requests make this connection demanding: an edit may select one occurrence, depend on a temporal relation, or modify a source that overlaps with other sounds. We introduce Harmony, an agentic framework that bridges audio understanding and editing through collaboration among an LLM planner, an audio-language model, and external tools. Harmony combines two mechanisms. Edit-driven collaborative planning uses targeted questions and tool measurements to determine the target, timing, and operation parameters. Evidence-guided execution uses observations of the first separated or generated audio to trigger bounded corrections before final mixing. Together, these mechanisms connect semantic decisions to waveform operations throughout the editing process. Harmony supports addition, removal, replacement, and volume adjustment. On 420 MMAE examples spanning these operations, Harmony achieves an exact match rate of 22.62%, compared with 13.57% for the strongest baseline, and improves aggregate instruction following and context preservation.
reasons: Audio Understanding & Reasoning: audio understanding
Audio & Speech Language Models: audio-language model

papers.title: Right Answers, Inconsistent Evidence: Source-Level Counterfactual Auditing of Large Audio-Language Models
papers.abstract: A large audio-language model (LALM) can answer "is a cat present?" about a mixture correctly, and its confidence can drop when the cat is removed, yet this does not show that it can tell the cat's presence from its absence. We introduce TRACE. It deletes the queried source and each rival in turn and asks whether every view still containing that sound outscores the view with it removed. Across 8 LALMs and 3,456 controlled mixtures, 6.3% of correct answers fail this ordering: the target-absent view scores at or above some target-present view, a conflict no shared threshold repairs. A target-only score check misses 42.5% of them. The share rises from 4.9% to 8.4% as target SNR falls from +5 to -5 dB, even on units correct at every level, and survives loudness and re-pairing controls. Accuracy certifies the answer; TRACE audits whether it orders presence above absence. Code and data: https://github.com/yikise/TRACE.

papers.title: Can Music Generation Models Tap Along? Evaluating Generative Approaches to Beat Tracking
papers.abstract: Existing studies have shown that music generative models can generate synchronized tracks that play alongside an input song. Can we extend this capability to develop a generative approach to beat tracking? To answer this question, we equip a pretrained MusicGen model with an audio-conditioning adapter to generate percussion tracks synchronized with the input music, from which we extract the beat positions. We train separate models with percussion targets of varying rhythmic complexity and compare them with two other generative models and conventional beat trackers. On GTZAN, our model achieves performance close to state-of-the-art beat trackers. Our model also demonstrates greater robustness: it shows the smallest drop in F-measure when drums are removed from the input at inference time. In certain genres, such as metal and disco, our model is also less likely to be misled by strong onsets or to miss beats with weak onsets. These results suggest that percussion generation has the potential to become a viable approach to beat tracking, and that its output is not merely a sequence of beat positions but an audible percussion track.
reasons: Generative Music & Audio: music generation, musicgen

papers.title: Speech Tokenizers are Vulnerable: Transferable Semantic Attack and Robust Tokenizer
papers.abstract: Speech tokenizers serve as speech front ends, encoding input speech signals into representations for downstream models, such as automatic speech recognition (ASR) systems and large audio-language models (LALMs). In this paper, we find that speech tokenizers are fragile at the semantic level: small perturbations can disrupt their semantic encoding process and consequently cause severe degradation in downstream ASR and LALM performance. To study this vulnerability, we propose T-SemAttack, a transferable semantic attack based on a semantic encoder ensemble. By jointly drifting the representation spaces of multiple semantic encoders, T-SemAttack effectively disrupts the semantic content of speech while preserving perceptual quality, thereby inducing error features. We further analyze layer-wise representation drift and cross-model gradient alignment. Our findings show that perturbations can induce substantial shifts in deep semantic representations and that the input gradients of different surrogate encoders exhibit directional alignment. These observations suggest that shared adversarially sensitive directions in the input space may be a key factor underlying cross-model attack transferability. Building on these, we introduce ROSETok, a robust speech tokenizer that combines noisy training with robust semantic distillation to improve reconstruction fidelity and downstream SpeechLLM robustness. Extensive experiments on multiple datasets, 9 open-source and black-box ASR systems, and 4 LALMs demonstrate that T-SemAttack achieves strong transferable attack performance, while the proposed Robust Speech Tokenizer exhibits robustness under high-fidelity reconstruction and downstream tasks. Our code and demo are available at https://wxzyd123.github.io/t-semattack.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio-language model
Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: automatic speech recognition

papers.title: RSE-TTS: Compact Text-to-Speech through Shared Text-Aware Reference Encoding and Generation
papers.abstract: Can a speech generator also serve as an effective voice encoder? We show that a pretrained autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) backbone can be repurposed for reference compression, improving speaker similarity in subsequent synthesis. Jointly encoding reference speech and its transcript further strengthens this capability. Controlled ablations and activation interventions trace the text benefit through intermediate acoustic representations into the compressed vectors that condition generation. Building on these findings, we introduce RSE-TTS, whose Reconstructive Speaker Encoder (RSE) shares the generation backbone and compresses paired reference text and speech into eight continuous vectors. Sharing reduces encoder-generator parameters by 48% relative to independent pretrained encoding. Large-scale English training yields a 118M-parameter generator that improves both word error rate and speaker similarity over the corresponding official MOSS-TTS-Nano cloning modes on all three English benchmarks. Combined with acoustic continuation, RSE-TTS approaches the speaker similarity of substantially larger systems while achieving lower WER than the evaluated CosyVoice 3 and MOSS-TTS-Local models. Audio samples are available at https://voxnexusai.github.io/RSE-TTS/.
papers.venue: 15 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Audio samples: https://voxnexusai.github.io/RSE-TTS/
reasons: Speech Generation, Recognition & Dialogue: text-to-speech

papers.title: CFGComposer: Compositional Audio-Text-to-Motion Generation via Copula Score Correction
papers.abstract: Generating whole-body gestures that are simultaneously rhythmically synchronized with speech audio and semantically aligned with text descriptions is a fundamental challenge in embodied AI and social robotics. We tackle this Audio-Text-to-Motion (AT2M) problem by composing two independently-trained diffusion models at inference time and refine bias in joint inference by modeling the copula score $s_I$. A rigorous theoretical analysis reveals that naive epsilon blending corresponds to a Product-of-Experts formulation that omits the copula score $s_I$: the cross-modal interaction between audio and text that neither marginal model can capture. We propose CFGComposer: a jointly-trained AT2M diffusion model that estimates $s_I$ via a CFG analogy and injects it as an $ε$-space correction. Experiments on BEAT demonstrate best-in-class semantic fidelity (SRGR $0.9916$, FID $27.18$) with GT-level beat alignment (BA $0.1826$ vs. GT $0.1743$), and 76-83% win rate in blind pairwise human evaluation against all prior methods. Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 humanoid confirms direct sim-to-real transfer.
reasons: Audio Understanding & Reasoning: audio-text

papers.title: Structured Speaker Conditioning for Diarization-Guided Target-Speaker ASR
papers.abstract: We propose structured speaker conditioning (SSC) for diarization-guided target-speaker recognition. SSC combines local activity structure with session-level acoustic identity to construct identity-consistent target conditions that control the acoustic encoder. Target-centric relational encoding (TCRE) retains per-speaker activity histories and factorized second- and third-order relations, capturing overlap and turn changes with aggregation cost linear in the number of tracks. Reference-based speaker conditioning (RSC) supplies session-derived identities that disambiguate local activity patterns within TCRE. Conditional low-rank modulation (CLRM) converts the joint condition into channel-wise affine modulation and a low-rank cross-channel residual with a condition-dependent core. On Qwen3-ASR-0.6B with oracle diarization, SSC uses 1.46M conditioning parameters and achieves a 6.23% mean relative reduction in concatenated minimum-permutation error rate (cpER) over four-state diagonal conditioning across four meeting test sets. SSC also transfers across audio foundation models. With predicted diarization and target-error group sequence policy optimization, the FireRedAudio text system achieves mean relative error reductions of 17.9% and 17.3% over DiCoW and MOSS-TD on the same four sets, and also outperforms both on three unseen domains. Scenario analyses identify gains under challenging overlap conditions, while fixed-checkpoint interventions support the contributions of session identity and the condition-dependent core. A timestamp variant jointly produces sentence boundaries and text. With predicted diarization, macro-average cpER across the four sets is 15.60% for text and 15.96% with timestamps.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio foundation model

papers.title: JEV-VAD: Efficient Semantic Endpointing via Task-First Conditioning and Decoder-Prefix Pruning
papers.abstract: Semantic endpointing must distinguish a completed turn from a temporary pause, yet its binary output does not require the full generation pathway of an audio-language model. We propose JEV-VAD, an ASR-free framework that combines task-first conditioning, a scalar endpoint readout, and decoder-prefix pruning. The question and completion criteria are placed before audio tokens, allowing causal decoder attention to construct audio states conditioned on the endpointing objective. A dedicated scalar head maps the assistant-prefix state directly to a stop probability, removing transcript generation, answer decoding, and vocabulary-sized output projection. To reduce representation cost, decoder-prefix pruning physically retains only the initial decoder blocks. Matched head refitting then identifies which retained depths provide useful endpoint information under a common adaptation budget. The framework is built on Qwen3-ASR-0.6B and adapted through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning for calibrated decisions. Together, these components address input conditioning, output complexity, and decoder depth within one endpointing framework. Experiments on EOT-bench show cross-language transfer from English endpoint supervision and useful discrimination in shallow prefixes, supporting a selectable quality-resource trade-off.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio-language model

papers.title: DeALR: Decoupled Audio-Latent Optimization with Acoustic Backtracking for Test-Time Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large audio-language models (LALMs) typically encode audio once and conduct subsequent multi-step reasoning in a language-dominated space, weakening access to fine-grained acoustic evidence. Although recent multimodal approaches have explored re-engaging perceptual inputs during reasoning, whether a frozen LALM can actively revisit crucial acoustic evidence in the latent space at test time remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, we introduce Decoupled Audio Latent Reasoning (DeALR), a novel test-time latent reasoning framework that shifts the paradigm from text-dominated deliberation to active audio-latent interaction. Inspired by the human cognitive process of "backtracking" to specific acoustic cues during complex listening tasks, DeALR establishes a dynamic interaction between learnable thought tokens and acoustic segments. Specifically, we introduce Span-Level Acoustic Backtracking, which traces initial attention distributions to dynamically isolate contiguous, key acoustic spans. Furthermore, we propose Decoupled Audio-Latent Optimization (DALO), a test-time reinforcement learning algorithm that jointly refines thought vectors and acoustic patches via confidence-guided policy gradients. Crucially, DALO explicitly decouples trajectory search from response generation by reinstating uncorrupted, high-fidelity audio embeddings prior to text synthesis, entirely eliminating optimization-induced distribution drift while retaining the navigation of the refined thoughts. Comprehensive experiments on benchmarks demonstrate that DeALR consistently outperforms prior test-time optimization approaches, delivering substantial improvements in both confidence calibration and reasoning accuracy.
reasons: Audio & Speech Language Models: audio-language model

## How to run

HeartMuLa-oss-3B (a 3B music language model: lyrics + style tags to song, with the HeartCodec audio codec), converted
for the MLX port in Moonbox's HeartMuLa engine. Each folder holds:

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `lm.safetensors` | the LM (backbone, depth decoder, codebook heads); MLX affine-quantized, group 64, in `8bit` / `6bit` / `4bit` |
| `quant.json` | which quantization the folder holds |
| `HeartCodec-decoder.safetensors` | the HeartCodec decoder (fp16) |
| `tokenizer.json`, `gen_config.json` | from HeartMuLa/HeartMuLaGen |

The layout is the one `audio/heartmula` in Moonbox reads; that runtime isn't part of this repository. No fp16 build:
the engine runs the LM in bf16.

**How they were checked.** Sampled songs differ from run to run, so every build scores the same codes instead: the
float32 model generates 12 s for 2 prompts (seed 0, CFG 1.5), then each build predicts every frame teacher-forced
(codebook 0 from the backbone, codebooks 1-7 from the depth decoder fed the true earlier codes, CFG as in generation).
Reported: KL(float32 || build) of the guided distributions and top-1 agreement with float32. Pass: mean KL <= 0.01
nats and agreement >= 90 %. The MLX port itself was checked against the official PyTorch pipeline when the engine was
written.

| Precision | Size | KL vs float32 (mean / p95) | Top-1 agreement (all / codebook 0) | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `bf16/` | 11.0 GB | 0.0016 / 0.0033 nats | 94.9 % / 95.3 % | passes |
| `8bit/` | 7.3 GB | 0.0020 / 0.0040 nats | 94.4 % / 96.3 % | passes |
| `6bit/` | 6.4 GB | 0.0066 / 0.0129 nats | 90.9 % / 93.3 % | passes |
| `4bit/` | 5.4 GB | 0.090 / 0.180 nats | 67.7 % / 85.0 % | **below threshold, experimental** |

## How these were made

From [HeartMuLa-oss-3B](https://huggingface.co/HeartMuLa/HeartMuLa-oss-3B) at revision `d12ac79c6b`: the original weights loaded in MLX and stored as bf16 or fp16, or
quantized with MLX's affine quantization (`8bit`, `6bit`, `4bit`, group size 64; layers MLX can't quantize, such as
convolutions and norms, stay bf16). Every build was checked against the original before upload; the `sha256` column
above is what the files must hash to.

## Model Description

**Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0** is an audio-capable version of [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1).
The model was developed by [LINAGORA](https://linagora.com) and
the [OpenLLM-France](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France) consortium, as part of the OpenLLM France project funded by
[BPI France](https://www.bpifrance.fr/) under the France 2030 program.

The training of Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0 was conducted on the Jean Zay supercomputer managed by [IDRIS](http://www.idris.fr/docs/idris/missions),
using the [NVIDIA NeMo Speech](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) toolkit.
The model was trained on various tasks and types of audio, including ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition), AST (Automatic Speech Translation), QA (Question Answering), Sound (Question Answering and Captioning), Music (Question Answering and Captioning) and more.

### Bias, Risks, and Limitations

- Inherits the limitations of the base [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1)
  language model: it can struggle with math word problems and is susceptible to hallucination.
- Training sequences were capped at 16,384 tokens (audio and text combined), so longer contexts are untested.
<!-- - The audio encoder and its front-end were entirely frozen during training, so audio understanding is bounded by what

## Training details

### Training data

Trained on the [OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset),
a large multilingual, multi-task collection of audio–text conversations comprising: ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition),
AST (Automatic Speech Translation), spoken question answering, summarization, diarization, temporal localization,
speaker/gender/age/emotion/language recognition, and music/sound captioning and QA (Question Answering).

### Instruction template

Same chat template as the base LLM (inspired by Qwen3), extended with an `<|audio|>` locator tag:
wherever `<|audio|>` appears in a turn, the corresponding audio segment is encoded and its embeddings
replace the tag before the sequence reaches the LLM. Conversations can carry several audio clips and mix
audio-only, text-only, and audio+text turns within the same dialogue (see the
[dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset) for example

| Component | Details |
|---|---|
| **Audio encoder** | [Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3) Conformer encoder, frozen |
| **RoTE** | Applied between audio encoder and audio adapter. θ=1200, rotary fraction=0.2. Inspired by [Goel et al., 2024, OMCAT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12109).|
| **Audio adapter** | Linear projection into the LLM embedding space (1024 -> 4096) |
| **LLM** | [Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Instruct-1.1), adapted with LoRA (on `q_proj`/`v_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`, r=64, α=64) |

| **Optimizer** | AdamW (β=(0.9, 0.98), weight decay 0.001) |
| **LR schedule** | Cosine annealing (max LR 2e-4, min LR 1e-6, 500 warmup steps) |
| **Batching** | Dynamic, bucketed by audio duration (27 buckets) |
| **Steps** | 100,000 |
| **Gradient clipping** | 1.0 |
| **Strategy** | FSDP2 (full sharding), activation checkpointing on the LLM (to allow for long sequences), 1 node × 4 H100 |
| **Precision** | bf16 |

```bash

```


```python
import base64
```

The model was trained on various tasks and types of audio, including ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition), AST (Automatic Speech Translation), QA (Question Answering), Sound (Question Answering and Captioning), Music (Question Answering and Captioning) and more.

If you are looking for the best compromise between speed and performance go check the [Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0).

  pipeline.

## Model Description

**Luciole-23B-Audio-1.0** is an audio-capable version of [Luciole-23B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-23B-Instruct-1.1).
The model was developed by [LINAGORA](https://linagora.com) and
the [OpenLLM-France](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France) consortium, as part of the OpenLLM France project funded by
[BPI France](https://www.bpifrance.fr/) under the France 2030 program.

The training of Luciole-23B-Audio-1.0 was conducted on the Jean Zay supercomputer managed by [IDRIS](http://www.idris.fr/docs/idris/missions),
using the [NVIDIA NeMo Speech](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) toolkit.
The model was trained on various tasks and types of audio, including ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition), AST (Automatic Speech Translation), QA (Question Answering), Sound (Question Answering and Captioning), Music (Question Answering and Captioning) and more.

If you are looking for the best compromise between speed and performance go check the [Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-8B-Audio-1.0).

### Bias, Risks, and Limitations

- Inherits the limitations of the base [Luciole-23B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-23B-Instruct-1.1)
  language model: it can struggle with math word problems and is susceptible to hallucination.
- Training sequences were capped at 16,384 tokens (audio and text combined), so longer contexts are untested.
<!-- - The audio encoder and its front-end were entirely frozen during training, so audio understanding is bounded by what
  Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 already hears: the model cannot learn to compensate for acoustic conditions the
  encoder itself handles poorly. -->
- Language coverage is uneven. French and English make up most of the training mix and are the only languages seen on every task. German, Spanish and Italian were seen in training for ASR, AST and spoken QA. Portuguese, Dutch and Arabic for ASR and AST only.
- Arabic is the weakest language: the frozen Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3 encoder was not trained on Arabic,
  so the model is clearly less reliable there (FLEURS WER ~25%).
<!-- - LoRA fine-tuning only touches attention projections in the LLM; no additional audio-specific safety or
  refusal tuning was performed beyond what the base LLM already has. -->

### Recommendations

- Speech, sound and music understanding (summarization, captioning, sound/music QA, conversation):
  best in French and English, the only languages the model was trained on for these tasks.
- Transcription (ASR) and translation (AST): supported in French, English, German, Spanish,
  Italian, Portuguese and Dutch. For production ASR/AST pipelines, a dedicated model may still
  perform better.
- Spoken question answering: mainly supported in French and English. German, Spanish and
  Italian are also supported, but with far less training data.
- Other languages and tasks: outside French and English, evaluate the model on your own data
  before relying on it, especially for a task the model was not trained on in that language.
- Up-to-date or domain-specific knowledge: as with the base LLM, pair the model with a RAG
  pipeline.

## Training details

### Training data

Trained on the [OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset),
a large multilingual, multi-task collection of audio–text conversations comprising: ASR (Automatic Speech Recognition),
AST (Automatic Speech Translation), spoken question answering, summarization, diarization, temporal localization,
speaker/gender/age/emotion/language recognition, and music/sound captioning and QA (Question Answering).

### Instruction template

Same chat template as the base LLM (inspired by Qwen3), extended with an `<|audio|>` locator tag:
wherever `<|audio|>` appears in a turn, the corresponding audio segment is encoded and its embeddings
replace the tag before the sequence reaches the LLM. Conversations can carry several audio clips and mix
audio-only, text-only, and audio+text turns within the same dialogue (see the
[dataset card](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training-Dataset) for example
conversations).

### Training Procedure

| Component | Details |
|---|---|
| **Audio encoder** | [Parakeet-TDT-0.6B-v3](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/parakeet-tdt-0.6b-v3) Conformer encoder, frozen |
| **RoTE** | Applied between audio encoder and audio adapter. θ=1200, rotary fraction=0.2. Inspired by [Goel et al., 2024, OMCAT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12109).|
| **Audio adapter** | Linear projection into the LLM embedding space (1024 -> 6144) |
| **LLM** | [Luciole-23B-Instruct-1.1](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-23B-Instruct-1.1), adapted with LoRA (on `q_proj`/`v_proj`, `up_proj`, `down_proj`, r=64, α=64) |
| **Trainable params** | 276M / ~24.1B (1.1%) |
| **Optimizer** | AdamW (β=(0.9, 0.98), weight decay 0.001) |
| **LR schedule** | Cosine annealing (max LR 2e-4, min LR 1e-6, 500 warmup steps) |
| **Batching** | Dynamic, bucketed by audio duration (27 buckets) |
| **Steps** | 100,000 |
| **Gradient clipping** | 1.0 |
| **Strategy** | FSDP2 (full sharding), activation checkpointing on the LLM (to allow for long sequences), 1 node × 4 H100 |
| **Precision** | bf16 |

The model was trained for 100k steps and drew from a weighted, randomly-ordered, sharded mix of that dataset,
bucketed by duration into 27 buckets (up to 1,200s / 16,384 audio-equivalent tokens per example) with a
matching dynamic batch size per bucket (238 down to 1).

Validation covered CommonVoice ASR (fr/en/ar),
Multilingual TEDx speech translation (fr→en), spoken QA (SLUE-SQA-5, VoxPopuli-QA, en/fr), and audio/music
captioning (AudioCaps, MusicCaps).

The training code and configs are available in the [Luciole-Audio-Training repository](https://github.com/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Training). Training used an updated version of [NeMo/Speech 3.1](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech) which can be found in our [NeMo/Speech fork](https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo/tree/luciole_speech.3.1.0-rc0).

## Evaluation

To evaluate our models and compare them with other open-weight Audio LLMs, we used [our fork of AudioBench](https://github.com/OpenLLM-France/AudioBench). We used a combination of datasets from AudioBench and datasets available in [our HF audio evaluation repository](https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-Audio-Evaluation-Dataset). You can find the full details and results on [our AudioBench leaderboard](https://openllm-france.github.io/AudioBench/).

A small excerpt from the leaderboard, showing the main table across all tasks and languages:

![results.png](assets/results.png)

Results for French and English only, as well as for ASR, AST, and QA tasks only:

![results_fr_en.png](assets/results_fr_en.png)

As you can see, the model [OpenLLM-France/Luciole-23B-Audio-1.0](https://huggingface.co/OpenLLM-France/Luciole-23B-Audio-1.0) performs well in French and English compared to other models.

For more detailed results in French ASR you can take a look at our [🏆 French ASR Leaderboard](https://linagora-labs.github.io/asr_benchmark/) where we use various types of datasets to evaluate the open source models. 

## Using the model

### With vLLM

The exported checkpoint's `config.json` declares `"model_type": "nemo_speechlm"` and
`"architectures": ["NeMoSpeechLMForConditionalGeneration"]`. Both are registered with vLLM by the SALM
plugin that ships inside `nemo-toolkit`
([`nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/tree/main/nemo/collections/speechlm2/vllm/salm))
via the `vllm.general_plugins` entry point:

```toml
[project.entry-points."vllm.general_plugins"]
nemo_speechlm = "nemo.collections.speechlm2.vllm.salm:register"
```

vLLM auto-discovers this plugin at startup as soon as `nemo-toolkit` and `vllm` are installed in the same
environment. The plugin merges the
LoRA adapters into the LLM backbone on load and runs the frozen Parakeet encoder + connector to turn each
`<|audio|>` tag into the right number of audio-embedding slots before generation.

**Install using uv**

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv pip install "nemo-toolkit[speechlm2,tts] @ git+https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo.git@luciole-1b-vllm-nemotron-fix"
uv pip install vllm==0.28.0
uv pip install "numpy<=2.4"
```

**Serve**

```bash
vllm serve OpenLLM-France/Luciole-23B-Audio-1.0 \
    --max-model-len 16384
```

**Query** (OpenAI-compatible chat API, audio sent as base64):

```python
import base64
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(base_url="http://localhost:8000/v1", api_key="EMPTY")

with open("sample.wav", "rb") as f:   # 16 kHz mono
    audio_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode()

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="OpenLLM-France/Luciole-23B-Audio-1.0",
    messages=[
        {
            "role": "user",
            "content": [
                {"type": "text", "text": "Transcris cet audio en français : <|audio|>"},
                {"type": "input_audio", "input_audio": {"data": audio_b64, "format": "wav"}},
            ],
        }
    ],
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
```

The `<|audio|>` placeholder is the same `audio_locator_tag` used during training: put it in the text
wherever the audio should be attended to; the plugin expands it automatically. Audio must be 16 kHz mono;
the encoder supports chunked processing for long-form audio (well beyond the durations seen in training).

### With NeMo

The checkpoint can also be loaded directly with NeMo's `SALM` class
([`nemo.collections.speechlm2.models.salm`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Speech/blob/main/nemo/collections/speechlm2/models/salm.py)).

**Install**

```bash
uv venv .venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

uv pip install "nemo-toolkit[speechlm2,tts] @ git+https://github.com/linagora-labs/NeMo.git@luciole-1b-vllm-nemotron-fix"
```

**Load and generate:**

```python
import torch
from nemo.collections.speechlm2 import SALM

model = SALM.from_pretrained("OpenLLM-France/Luciole-23B-Audio-1.0")  # or a local checkpoint directory
model = model.eval().to(torch.bfloat16).to("cuda")

# High-level API: pass the audio file path(s) directly in the prompt, next to the
# `<|audio|>` placeholder; SALM loads and resamples the audio for you.
answer_ids = model.generate(
    prompts=[
        [
            {
                "role": "user",
                "content": f"Transcris cet audio en français : {model.audio_locator_tag}",
                "audio": ["sample.wav"],
            }
        ]
    ],
    max_new_tokens=256,
)
print(model.tokenizer.ids_to_text(answer_ids[0].tolist()))
```

A prompt can carry several turns and several audio clips (one `<|audio|>` tag per clip, in order).

### Example prompts for each task

- ASR: 
  - English: `Make a word-for-word transcription in English of the spoken content.`
  - French: `Fais une transcription mot pour mot en français du contenu parlé.`
  - German: `Erstelle eine wortwörtliche Transkription des gesprochenen Inhalts auf Deutsch.`
  - Spanish: `Haz una transcripción palabra por palabra en español del contenido hablado.`
  - Italian: `Fai una trascrizione parola per parola in italiano del contenuto parlato.`
  - Portuguese: `Faça uma transcrição palavra por palavra em português do conteúdo falado.`
  - Dutch: `Maak een woord-voor-woord transcriptie in het Nederlands van de gesproken inhoud.`
  - No language given: `Can you write the text of this audio file in its source language?`
- QA: `Listen to the audio and answer the question.`
- AST: `Translate this file into French.`
- Diarization: 
  - `Provide a time-stamped, speaker-attributed transcript of this audio.`
  - `Transcris et diarise cet enregistrement, avec les horodatages de chaque tour.`

> Ruach Studio is open music generation that runs on your own hardware: the model, the score, the adapters and every take stay yours, and nothing is rented by the token. Open models are now good enough to stand on their own, and what was missing is the studio around them: that is what we build, in the open. Music should be free to make and to share: whoever has no voice, no instrument and no studio still has the right to lay their thoughts and feelings onto sound. > **⚠ Not on free cloud GPUs.** Ruach Studio does not run on Google Colab, Kaggle or any free notebook GPU, so don't spend an evening on it there: it is a whole studio, not a notebook. It builds its C++/CUDA engine on the machine it lives on, keeps a server and a lab of Python services running beside it, and takes about 33 GB of disk (60 GB with the Artist). A free session's card, memory, wiped disk and hours-long limit cannot hold that. It wants your own Linux computer, or a server you rent and keep, with an NVIDIA card: 24 GB for everything, 16 GB with the smaller model copies. # 👑 JJ coders Suna AI v1.0 — Official Halloween 2026 Flagship Foundation Model

**JJ coders Suna AI v1.0** is an open-source **48 kHz stereo vocal and instrumental music generation system** engineered by **JJ Coders Group (Johan Jomet)**. # StaleyNET checkpoints

[![Source on GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/source-GitHub-1D1B20?logo=github)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet) [![staleynet-audio on crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/staleynet-audio?label=staleynet-audio)](https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio) [![Paper](https://img.shields.io/badge/paper-PDF-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/blob/main/paper/preprint.pdf) [![Book](https://img.shields.io/badge/book-mdBook-6750A4)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/tree/main/book/src) [![Release v0.1.2](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/arpanpathak/staleynet)](https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases) [![Dataset: 3.1 GB](https://img.shields.io/badge/dataset-3.1%20GB-FFD21E?logo=huggingface&logoColor=black)](https://huggingface.co/datasets/arpanpathak/staleynet-data)

Weights for **StaleyNET**, a text-prompted music generator trained from random initialization in Rust on NVIDIA edge GPUs. The Transformer, residual vector quantizer, Griffin-Lim vocoder, and GPU kernels are implemented in the project.

The code, paper, and book live in the companion repository:
<https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet>.

## Release v0.1.2

- GitHub release: <https://github.com/arpanpathak/staleynet/releases/tag/v0.1.2>
- `staleynet-audio` 0.1.2 on crates.io: <https://crates.io/crates/staleynet-audio>. Its page explains each audio step with intuition and runnable examples.
- Since v0.1.1: the GPU kernels are organised into one module per topic, the AGX Thor builds against cuda-oxide's main branch, and the paper has been revised with hardware, benchmark and tokenizer appendices.
- New in these repositories: the `lyrics-thor`, `lyrics-thor-long` and `pq-large` runs, and the band-group token caches they train on.
- CI: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, cargo-deny, the audio coverage gate, and documentation tests for every example on the crate page.

## At a glance

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Checkpointed runs | 9 |
| Parameters | 7,099,904 for text-only runs; 7,165,440 for the lyrics runs; 42,858,496 for `pq-large` |
| Transformer | width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, context 768 (`pq-large`: width 512, 8 layers, context 1152) |
| Audio tokens | 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries (`pq-large`: 4 band groups × 4 levels = 16 codebooks of 1024 entries) |
| Audio features | 128 mel bands at 24 kHz, FFT 1024, hop 256 |
| Training data | Song Describer Dataset and JamendoLyrics MultiLang |
| License | CC BY-SA 4.0, subject to the upstream dataset terms |

## Checkpoints

| Run | Purpose | Parameters | `best` step | `latest` step | Training tracks |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| `thor-base` | base text-to-music model | 7,099,904 | 0 | None | 667 |
| `smoke` | pipeline smoke test | 7,099,904 | 0 | 1,500 | 667 |
| `overfit-one-take` | single-take memorisation check | 7,099,904 | 200 | 200 | 1 |
| `vocal-scratch` | vocal-filtered model from scratch | 7,099,904 | 5,500 | 6,000 | 281 |
| `vocal-finetune` | vocal fine-tune | 7,099,904 | 250 | None | 281 |
| `lyrics-orin` | lyrics-conditioned model | 7,165,440 | 3,750 | 4,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor` | lyrics-conditioned model trained on the AGX Thor | 7,165,440 | 4,750 | 8,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `lyrics-thor-long` | the same model trained for 20,000 steps | 7,165,440 | 19,750 | 20,000 | 543 (73 with lyrics) |
| `pq-large` | larger model on the band-group tokenizer (in progress) | 42,858,496 | 7,000 | 7,000 | 742 (75 with lyrics) |

The step values are exactly what each `model.json` records. `best/` is the weight-only checkpoint selected by validation. `latest/` is the resumable checkpoint with AdamW moments. Some early runs stored only `best/`, and `thor-base` and `smoke` record step 0 in their `best/model.json`. Where a `latest/` exists, prefer it for the late training state.

### About `pq-large`

`pq-large` is still training on the Jetson AGX Thor (128 GB). The files here are a snapshot at step 7,000 of 20,000, and they will be replaced as the run advances. Its validation loss (5.135 nats per token at step 7,000) is averaged over 16 codebooks of a different tokenizer, so it cannot be compared directly with the 4-codebook runs above.

The model reads codes from the band-group tokenizer, which splits the 128 mel bands into 4 groups and quantises each group with 4 residual levels. That tokenizer is stored as `checkpoints/pq-large/tokenizer.json`, and the matching caches are `cache-g4l4f1/`, `cache-pq-jamendolyrics/` and `cache-pq-recordings/` in the dataset repository. Pass `--cache data/cache-g4l4f1` when generating with this run.

`evaluations/<run>/` holds the paired lyrics test of each lyrics run: the per-track loss with aligned, removed and mismatched lyrics.

## Training progress

The runs on the Jetson AGX Thor publish their metrics here every two hours
(`deploy/hf/publish.sh` in the code repository): `metrics/<run>.jsonl` holds
every logged event, and `plots/<run>.png` shows, from left to right, the
training and validation loss in nats per code against optimizer step, the
latest validation loss of each codebook (coarse levels are far easier to
predict than fine ones), and the throughput in positions per second.

![pq-large training curves](plots/pq-large.png)

## Layout

```text
checkpoints/<run>/best/      weights only       model.json + tensors.bin
checkpoints/<run>/latest/    weights + AdamW    model.json + tensors.bin
configs/                     canonical training configurations
run-configs/                 per-run config.json where the run saved one
metrics/                     full metrics.jsonl for every run
logs/                        captured training logs and the tokenizer sweeps
evaluations/<run>/           paired lyrics evaluations
```

`tensors.bin` is little-endian `f32` in parameter-visitor order. `latest/` appends the AdamW first moments and then the second moments. `model.json` records the tensor manifest, the step, whether optimizer state is present, and the training configuration.

## Download and use

```bash
hf download arpanpathak/staleynet-checkpoints \
  --repo-type model --local-dir staleynet-checkpoints

# From the code repository, on a Jetson with the cuda-oxide toolchain:
cargo oxide build -- --release
staleynet sing \
  --cache data/cache \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/thor-base/best \
  --prompt "slow acoustic ballad, warm female voice" \
  --out song.wav
```

For the lyrics model:

```bash
staleynet sing \
  --run staleynet-checkpoints/checkpoints/lyrics-orin/best \
  --prompt "grunge rock, raw male voice" \
  --lyrics-file song.txt \
  --out song.wav
```

Architecture: width 256, 8 heads, 6 layers, feed-forward multiplier 4, context length 768, 4 residual codebooks of 1024 entries, 128 mel bands at 24 kHz. `lyrics-orin` adds a 256-byte lyrics field.

## Training data and licensing

- **Song Describer Dataset** (SDD), Zenodo record [10072001](https://zenodo.org/records/10072001): 706 Jamendo recordings with human captions. Captions are CC BY-SA 4.0. The recordings carry the per-track Creative Commons licenses in `audio_licenses.txt`, including CC BY-NC-ND and CC BY-NC-SA.
- **JamendoLyrics MultiLang**, <https://github.com/f90/jamendolyrics>: code and metadata are MIT. Songs and lyrics carry the per-song CC licenses in `JamendoLyrics.csv`.

Because the training audio includes NonCommercial and NoDerivatives tracks, these checkpoints are research artifacts, not a commercial product. Do not use them commercially where the upstream recording licenses forbid it, and do not use them to impersonate a singer without consent.

The checkpoint files are offered under CC BY-SA 4.0 (`LICENSE-CC-BY-SA-4.0.txt`) to the extent the upstream dataset licenses allow. See `NOTICE` for the full provenance statement and `SHA256SUMS` for integrity.

## Known limitations

- Griffin-Lim produces phasey audio compared with a learned vocoder.
- The models are small edge models, not production music systems.
- The lyric models were trained on a small lyrics subset, so lyric intelligibility is limited.
- The checkpoints are research artifacts and have no warranty.

# YuE2-3B · IRA and IRAE merges

> Ruach Studio is open music generation that runs on your own hardware: the model, the score, the adapters and every take stay yours, and nothing is rented by the token. Open models are now good enough to stand on their own, and what was missing is the studio around them: that is what we build, in the open. Music should be free to make and to share: whoever has no voice, no instrument and no studio still has the right to lay their thoughts and feelings onto sound.

> **⚠ Not on free cloud GPUs.** Ruach Studio does not run on Google Colab, Kaggle or any free notebook GPU, so don't spend an evening on it there: it is a whole studio, not a notebook. It builds its C++/CUDA engine on the machine it lives on, keeps a server and a lab of Python services running beside it, and takes about 33 GB of disk (60 GB with the Artist). A free session's card, memory, wiped disk and hours-long limit cannot hold that. It wants your own Linux computer, or a server you rent and keep, with an NVIDIA card: 24 GB for everything, 16 GB with the smaller model copies. The weights on this page load wherever YuE2-3B does, ComfyUI among them: the warning is about the studio.

**IRA** stands for **I**nstrumental + **R**eal **A**udio. Two community LoRAs are folded into the weights of [m-a-p's YuE2-3B](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-3B), so the model plays them with no adapter loaded. The merge was made and checked in [Ruach Studio](https://github.com/igrbible/Ruach_Studio), a free studio built on YuE2 ([its page](https://ruachstudio.art)).

| adapter | author | half of YuE2 | strength |
|---|---|---|---|
| [YuE2-instrumental-cot-full-loras](https://huggingface.co/Mothersuperior/YuE2-instrumental-cot-full-loras) · `ar_lora_inst_v3abc` | Mothersuperior | music (AR: the score and the music tokens) | 0.75 |
| [yue2-mothersuperior-realaudio-tokenizer-v4](https://huggingface.co/Mothersuperior/yue2-mothersuperior-realaudio-tokenizer-v4) · `nar_lora_joint_v9` | Mothersuperior | sound (NAR: the decoder of the latents) | 0.85 |

The Instrumental adapter gives the music half a feel for arrangement and section plans. The Real Audio adapter moves the sound half toward real-production recordings.

## IRAE: IRA with an epic-trailer adapter

**IRAE** is IRA plus [monsterovich's Epic Trailer adapter](https://huggingface.co/monsterovich/yue2-steps-from-hell) (`yue2-steps-from-hell`: a music-half file, `adapter-ar-195`, and a sound-half file, `adapter-nar-194`). Three strengths, all heard and kept:

| merge | Epic Trailer, music / sound | by ear |
|---|---|---|
| **IRAE** | 0.32 / 0.32 | the best of the three |
| **IRAEv2** | 0.28 / 0.24 | cleaner |
| **IRAEv3** | 0.5 / 0.375, the strengths its author recommends | more grain in the voice; at its best on instrumentals |

Every IRAE carries IRA whole (Instrumental 0.75 on the music half, Real Audio v9 0.85 on the sound half). All four adapters were added in one pass from the stock BF16, in F32, exactly as IRA was made.

- **Measured:** the Epic Trailer's music half at 1.0 broke every score (9 plans out of 9 had no key line). At 0.5 and below the scores held (18 out of 18 for IRAEv2 and IRAEv3). Its sound half raised the hiss in the quietest fifth even at 0.32–0.4, and the ear still preferred it.
- **Do not load Epic Trailer again on top of an IRAE,** nor Instrumental or Real Audio: they are inside.

## IRAE-IR and IRAE-IRv2: experimental, for rock instrumentals

> ⚠ **Highly unstable on lyrics. Experimental: mostly for rock instrumentals.**

**IRAE-IR** is IRAE plus [monsterovich's Industrial Rock adapter](https://huggingface.co/monsterovich/yue2-industrial-rock-lora) (`yue2-industrial-rock-lora`: a music-half file, `adapter-ar-179`, and a sound-half file, `adapter-nar-179-v2`). Each carries IRAE whole (IRA plus Epic Trailer 0.32 / 0.32); all six adapters were added in one pass from the stock BF16, in F32.

| merge | Industrial Rock, music / sound | by ear |
|---|---|---|
| **IRAE-IR** | 0.4 / 0.6 | richer than IRA and IRAE, with the rock colour the adapter brings, and raw rock sounds good; the words are what suffers: the phonetics get worse, the voice can drown in the band, a ballad can lose words and its feel. A sung poem over a duduk came out well |
| **IRAE-IRv2** | 0.32 / 0.6 | the music half lowered further for steadier words; made after that verdict, not yet heard |

- **Measured:** Industrial Rock's music half at 0.6 broke two plans out of seven (no key line); its limit measured at 0.45, and both merges stay under it.
- **Do not load Industrial Rock again on top,** nor Epic Trailer, Instrumental or Real Audio: they are inside.

## Files

| file | for | size |
|---|---|---|
| `model.safetensors` + `config.json`, `modeling_yue2.py`, `qwen.tiktoken`, the generation configs | anything that loads m-a-p/YuE2-3B (Transformers with `trust_remote_code`, ComfyUI conversions, your own code): the same layout and names, BF16 | 7.3 GB |
| `YuE2-3B-IRA-BF16.gguf` | [yue2.cpp](https://github.com/ServeurpersoCom/yue2.cpp) and Ruach Studio, the whole merge | 7.2 GB |
| `YuE2-3B-IRA-Q8_0.gguf` | the same, quantized from the merged BF16 | 3.8 GB |
| `YuE2-3B-IRA-Q6_K.gguf` | the same, smaller | 2.9 GB |

The three IRAE merges sit beside IRA in the same three GGUF sizes: `YuE2-3B-IRAE-BF16.gguf`, `YuE2-3B-IRAE-Q8_0.gguf`, `YuE2-3B-IRAE-Q6_K.gguf`, and the same for `IRAEv2`, `IRAEv3`, `IRAE-IR` and `IRAE-IRv2`. Their safetensors are in the folders `IRAE/`, `IRAEv2/`, `IRAEv3/`, `IRAE-IR/` and `IRAE-IRv2/`, each in m-a-p's layout: load one with `subfolder="IRAE"`.

The VAE is not part of this repo. Use m-a-p's [YuE2-Vae](https://huggingface.co/m-a-p/YuE2-Vae) as before; in GGUF form it is in [Serveurperso/YuE2-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/Serveurperso/YuE2-GGUF).

**Do not load these two adapters again on top of IRA.** They are already inside, and loading them again would double them. Other adapters stack as usual.

## How it was merged

- Both adapters were taken in their fp32 files (`ar_lora_inst_v3abc.safetensors`, `nar_lora_joint_v9.safetensors`), not their bf16 copies: they are only merged, never loaded, so the larger file costs nothing.
- Each LoRA pair was added as `W + strength × alpha/rank × B @ A` in F32 and stored back in BF16. The arithmetic is yue2.cpp's own LoRA merge (its `lora.h`): the merged BF16 GGUF loads into the same weights as the stock model with these two adapters at these strengths at load time.
- Real Audio ships full `vae2llm` / `llm2vae` weights rather than a low-rank pair. At 0.85 they enter as `base + 0.85 × (theirs − base)`, as yue2.cpp applies them.
- The quants were made from the merged BF16 (yue2.cpp's `quantize`), not by merging into a quant.
- `model.safetensors` is m-a-p's own file with the 396 merged tensors taken from the BF16 GGUF. It was checked tensor by tensor after writing: the 2-D weights are the GGUF's bit for bit, and the two biases are rounded to BF16 as m-a-p stores them.

## What we measured (preliminary)

These are first numbers from two prompts, an epic instrumental and a sung Russian ballad, taken on RTX 3090s in October 2026. They are a start, not a verdict.

- **Exactness.** The merged BF16 GGUF and the stock BF16 with the two adapters at runtime gave the same audio and the same latents, byte for byte (same score, same seeds).
- **The score holds.** Three prompts × three seeds on the BF16, the Q8_0 and the Q6_K all wrote a valid ABC score (key, meter, note length): 36 plans, none broken. Only the music half writes the score, and it is the same in IRA and in the neighbouring recipe whose quants were planned (Real Audio at 0.9).
- **Sound.** The hiss in the quietest fifth of each take was not above the stock model's, and the 2–6 kHz share stayed at 1–4 % of the energy. Recipes that carried an epic-trailer adapter raised both, even at 0.32–0.4.
- **By ear.** Approved for release. It is strongest on sung songs; a pure instrumental can carry a little noise.

If you hear it differently, tell us. The numbers are ours, not laws.

## Use

- **Ruach Studio:** Engine › Models and LoRAs › More models › «IRA merge» (and, from 2.0.0, «IRAE», «IRAEv2», «IRAEv3», «IRAE-IR», «IRAE-IRv2») fetches a GGUF. Engine › Compute then chooses it beside m-a-p's weights.
- **yue2.cpp:** pass the GGUF as the backbone (`--model YuE2-3B-IRA-Q8_0.gguf`), with the stock VAE.
- **Transformers and other shells:** load this repo as you load `m-a-p/YuE2-3B`.

# TuneJury — instance-level pairwise reward model for text-to-music

TuneJury is a 2.8M-parameter MLP head over frozen LAION-CLAP-Music + MERT-v1-330M
embeddings, trained with a shared-weight pairwise-logistic objective on ~17.5K human
A vs. B preferences from four open sources. It scores a single audio clip (with an
optional text prompt) as one preference scalar.

- **Paper:** https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17006
- **Project Page:** https://yonghyunk1m.github.io/TuneJury/
- **Code:** https://github.com/yonghyunk1m/TuneJury
- **Demo:** https://huggingface.co/spaces/TuneJury/tune-jury-demo
- **Scope:** trained and evaluated on instrumental music. For prompt formats unlike the
  live-arena style it was trained on (e.g. post-hoc captions), an empty prompt can be the
  safer default (paper §4.2). Anchor calibration adapts to newly released generators
  without retraining.

## Checkpoints

| File | Encoder / mix | License |
|---|---|---|
| `tunejury.pt` | CLAP+MERT, 4-dataset (primary) | CC-BY-NC 4.0 |
| `tunejury_muq_leave_MA.pt` | MuQ-MuLan-large encoder-swap | CC-BY-NC 4.0 |
| `A1_clap_audio_only.pt` | CLAP-audio-only | Apache-2.0 |
| `B1L_clap2_large_audio_only.pt` | CLAP2-Large audio-only, 4-dataset (new) | Apache-2.0 |
| `B1S_clap2_small_audio_only.pt` | CLAP2-Small audio-only, 4-dataset (new) | Apache-2.0 |
| `B2S_clap2_small_audio_text.pt` | CLAP2-Small audio + text prompt, 4-dataset (new) | Apache-2.0 |
| `tunejury_leave_*.pt` | leave-one / leave-two-out (fair-eval) | CC-BY-NC 4.0 |

## Quick scoring

Install the package (also pulls the LAION-CLAP encoder ~2.2 GB on first use; needs
`ffmpeg` and `libsndfile`):

```bash
pip install git+https://github.com/yonghyunk1m/TuneJury
```

```python
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from tunejury.score import Scorer

sc = Scorer.from_pretrained(hf_hub_download("TuneJury/tunejury", "tunejury.pt"))
print(sc.score("clip.wav", ""))   # "" -> 512-d zero text vector (paper §3/§4.2 empty-prompt)
print(sc.score("clip.wav", "a calm lo-fi piano loop"))   # a prompt uses the text branch
```

## CLAP2 heads (B1L, B1S audio-only; B2S audio + text)

Three additional heads over the frozen [LAION CLAP2](https://huggingface.co/laion/clap2-large-audioxl-s1B)
Large and Small models. LAION reports 340.1M and 103.9M parameters for these models, counting both
the audio and the text tower. B1L and B1S read only the audio tower (166.5M and 41.8M parameters).
B2S also reads the prompt through the CLAP2-Small text tower (62.1M parameters), so it uses the
whole 103.9M-parameter model. All three use the primary head's MLP, training pairs, objective and
hyperparameters (seed 42). Only the input differs. B1L and B1S take one CLAP2 audio embedding,
with no MERT and no text. B2S appends the L2-normalised CLAP2 text embedding of the prompt, or a
zero vector when the prompt is empty. All three have an Apache-2.0 head and encoder. The existing
checkpoints are unchanged.

Same evaluation code for every row. "MA 2026-02/03" is the 799 decisive Feb–Mar 2026 Music
Arena battles, collected after the training cutoff.

Internal, MA and CMI-Pref columns report pairwise accuracy. Over three training seeds the CLAP2-L
audio-only configuration averages PAM 0.668 ± 0.034 and MusicEval 0.723 ± 0.010, versus
0.568 ± 0.017 and 0.552 ± 0.033 for LAION-CLAP audio-only. PAM and MusicEval values can differ by
up to about 0.03 from the official CMI-RewardBench harness, which applies its own clip-length cap.
With prompts, the B2S configuration averages CMI MA 0.722 ± 0.007 and CMI-Pref 0.751 ± 0.010 over
the same three seeds, but MusicEval only 0.580 ± 0.034. Use B2S when a
prompt is available and the audio-only heads otherwise. MusicEval has no prompts, so both B2S rows
share its value.

Features must match training. Decode at the native sample rate (no 16 kHz step) and mix to mono.
Split the clip into non-overlapping 30 s windows from the start, at most four. Average the

```bash
python clap2_only.py clip.wav --size small-text --text "calm solo piano"   # B2S
```

[CLAP2_ONLY.md](https://huggingface.co/spaces/TuneJury/tune-jury/blob/main/CLAP2_ONLY.md).

The upstream card is the > authoritative source. # Granite-Speech-4.1-2B **Model Summary:** Granite Speech 4.1 2B is a compact and efficient speech-language model, specifically designed for multilingual automatic speech recognition (ASR) and bidirectional automatic speech translation (AST) for English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese and Japanese. Granite Speech 4.1 2B was trained by modality aligning an intermediate checkpoint of [granite-4.0-1b-base](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-1b-base) to speech on publicly available open source corpora containing audio inputs and text targets. Compared to its predecessor [granite-4.0-1b-speech](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-4.0-1b-speech), this model has the same parameter count (the new naming convention reflects actual instead of base LLM size) and provides additional capabilities and improvements: * Higher transcription accuracy for multilingual ASR due to a novel dual-head CTC encoder with both graphemic and BPE outputs and frame importance sampling to focus on informative parts of the audio * Punctuation and truecasing for ASR and AST in all languages (including German noun capitalization) with a simple prompt change * Better keyword list biasing capability for enhanced recognition of names, acronyms and technical jargon Two additional model variants explore different capabilities and inference optimization: * [granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus) adds speaker-attributed ASR and word-level time stamps * [granite-speech-4.1-2b-nar](https://huggingface.co/ibm-granite/granite-speech-4.1-2b-nar) introduces a novel non-autoregressive architecture for higher throughput **Evaluations:** We evaluated granite-speech-4.1-2b alongside other speech-language models in the less than 8b parameter range as well as dedicated ASR and AST systems on standard benchmarks. The evaluation spanned multiple public benchmarks, with particular emphasis on English ASR tasks while also including multilingual ASR and AST for X-En and En-X translations.

It is a pretrained base model, released for research. - **Native full-duplex at 7.5 Hz.** Every 133 ms the model takes one frame of the user's audio and produces one frame of its own audio and text. User audio, model audio and model text are summed into a single position of the language model, so listening and speaking never wait for each other. - **Continuous audio, one sampling step.** Audio is a 64-dimensional latent per frame. A small MLP head with MeanFlow sampling produces it in one step from the language model's hidden state; there is no separate audio transformer and there are no discrete audio tokens. - **Character and voice control.** A text card sets the character, a short reference clip sets the voice. - **Multilingual.** English, Spanish, Portuguese, German, French, Chinese, Japanese, Russian and Korean.

## Usage The code is at : a PyTorch implementation with a web demo, an MLX implementation with a native macOS app, and a plugin for serving with vLLM-Omni. With an NVIDIA GPU (about 12 GB of memory): ```bash git clone https://github.com/higurashi-ai/Haru && cd Haru pip install -e ./haru python -m haru.server --hf-repo higurashi-ai/Haru-4B ``` Open , pick a character, give the model a voice, and talk. For low latency, we recommend wired headphones and a wired microphone. Bluetooth devices add 100 ms or more. **Bring your own voice.** Haru ships without voice clips. Upload or record a clip of the voice the model should speak with: one speaker, 3 seconds to 3 minutes, clean speech. Only use voices you have the right to use. ```python from haru import DuplexSession, HaruModel from haru.audio import load_audio, prepare_reference model = HaruModel.from_pretrained("higurashi-ai/Haru-4B") voice = prepare_reference(load_audio("voice.wav")) session = DuplexSession(model, system_prompt=card, reference=voice) frame = session.start() # the model's first 133 ms: frame.audio, frame.text while not frame.done: frame = session.step(user_audio) # 3200 samples at 24 kHz in, 3200 out ``` The system prompt is a character card with a fixed layout; the repository's README shows how to build one. ## Files | File | Contents | | --- | --- | | `model.safetensors` | All weights (bfloat16): `lm.*` language model, `model_audio_proj.*` / `user_audio_proj.*` audio input projections, `head.*` MeanFlow head, `codec.*` audio codec | | `config.json` | Model configuration | | `tokenizer.json` | Text tokenizer | ## Architecture | Part | Details | | --- | --- | | Language model | Qwen3.5-4B text backbone, 32 layers, hidden size 2560 | | Audio codec | VibeVoice acoustic tokenizer, causal, 24 kHz, 3200 samples per latent | | Audio head | 4-layer MLP, MeanFlow, 1 sampling step, guidance scale 1 to 2 (default 1.5) | | Frame rate | 7.5 Hz | ## Limitations Haru-4B is a pretrained base model, released for research. It holds a natural conversation, but it is not a reliable source of facts and does not follow instructions the way an assistant does. It can imitate the voice of a reference clip; only use voices you have the right to use. ## License The weights are released under the Apache License 2.0.

--- ZONOS3-Mini is Zyphra’s compact, open-source text-to-speech model, delivering natural reliable speech and high-fidelity voice cloning with just 100 million active parameters. It runs in real time on phones and laptops, including directly in the browser. Clone a voice from an audio sample, or design a character by shaping age, accent and vocal texture. Steer emotion, pace and delivery down to individual words for games, narration and voice assistants. Run ZONOS3-Mini locally with our browser and native runtimes, or access it through [Zyphra Cloud](https://cloud.zyphra.com/models/zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini). Model weights are released under Apache 2.0. **Model details, samples and evaluations are in the [blog post](https://www.zyphra.com/our-work/zonos3-mini).** **A hosted version is available at [Zyphra Cloud](https://cloud.zyphra.com/models/zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini).** ## Languages ZONOS3-Mini supports 43 languages. | Region | Languages | |---|---| | Western and Southern Europe | English, French, Spanish, German, Italian, Portuguese, Dutch, Greek | | Northern Europe | Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, Finnish | | Central and Eastern Europe | Polish, Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, Romanian, Bulgarian, Russian, Ukrainian | | Middle East and Caucasus | Turkish, Arabic, Hebrew, Georgian | | East Asia | Mandarin Chinese, Japanese, Korean | | Southeast Asia | Vietnamese, Indonesian, Malay, Thai, Tagalog | | South Asia | Hindi, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu, Marathi, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Punjabi, Odia, Urdu | ## Quick start ### In your browser ZONOS3-Mini runs entirely on your own GPU through WebGPU: no install and no server. The first visit downloads the model, and the browser keeps it cached for later visits. You need a browser with WebGPU support. - [Zonos Voice Studio](https://zyphra.com/zonos3-mini/localplayground#cast): the full studio. - [Lite](https://zyphra.com/zonos3-mini/localplayground/lite): quick voice cloning. Pick, upload or record a voice and speak with it. ### With SGLang [SGLang-Omni](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni) serves ZONOS3-Mini on NVIDIA GPUs behind the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/audio/speech` endpoint, with streaming and voice cloning from a reference clip (no transcript needed). Install SGLang-Omni by following its [installation guide](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/get_started/installation.md), then start a server: ```bash sgl-omni serve --model-path Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini --port 8000 ``` Once `curl http://localhost:8000/health` reports `"healthy"`, generate speech with the default voice from another terminal: ```bash curl -X POST http://localhost:8000/v1/audio/speech \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"input": "Hello from ZONOS3-Mini!"}' \ --output output.wav ``` Add `"references": [{"audio_path": ""}]` to clone a voice, or `"stream": true, "response_format": "pcm"` to stream 44.1 kHz audio as it is generated. The [ZONOS3 cookbook](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang-omni/blob/main/docs/cookbook/zonos3.md) covers voice cloning, streaming and the sampling options. ### Native runtimes The [ZONOS3-Mini GitHub repository](https://github.com/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini) holds Zyphra's own runtimes, which share one HTTP API and serve the Zonos Voice Studio: a CUDA server for NVIDIA GPUs, an MLX server for Apple Silicon, a C++/ggml server and CLI (CPU, CUDA, Metal or Vulkan), and the in-browser WebGPU build. They load the GGUF files in [`gguf/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/tree/main/gguf) and the WebGPU shards in [`web/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/tree/main/web); the 27 default voices, grouped by language, are in [`gguf/voices/`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/blob/main/gguf/voices/README.md). ## Architecture (rough outline) Text is NeMo-normalized (English, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, German, Spanish, French, Italian, Portuguese; other languages pass through as written) and encoded with an 8,192-entry SuperBPE tokenizer. The language model autoregressively generates 15 Hz dual-codec frames (10 codebooks of 4,096 entries each: one semantic codebook distilled from the Wav2Vec2-BERT teacher plus nine acoustic codebooks), conditioned on the text, a speaker prompt and three bucketed acoustic controls. A causal multi-resolution iSTFT head renders the frames to 44.1 kHz audio as they are produced. ![ZONOS3-Mini inference pipeline](assets/zonos3_mini_arloop_animated.gif) *Inference pipeline. Speaker conditioning (raw reference codes or a speaker-embedding row), control rows and SuperBPE text enter the hybrid GDN/attention MoE backbone, which predicts all ten codebooks of the next frame under the delay pattern (four drawn); as soon as a frame's last codebook is generated, the codec's causal iSTFT head renders that frame to audio.* | | ZONOS3-Mini | |---|---| | Backbone | 11 layers, model dim 1,024; 800M parameters total, about 100M active per token (latent MoE: 64 experts, top-2 routing, from layer 1) | | Sequence mixer | pattern `gdn3_global1`: 9 Gated DeltaNet (GDN) layers + 2 global attention layers (16 heads x 32 dims, 4 KV heads), attention residuals (`full_attnres`); context 32,768 positions | | Text | SuperBPE, 8,192 entries (+4 specials), NeMo text normalization at inference | | Audio tokens | 15 Hz, 44.1 kHz dual-encoding codec, 10 x 4,096 codebooks (1 semantic + 9 acoustic); hop 2,940 samples; up to 10 minutes of audio per generation | | Speaker prompt | raw reference clip (encoded by the codec into a token prefix, up to 60 s, with speaker CFG) **or** a single 192-d MECT-B2 speaker embedding (`ownmect_s2`) | | Controls | loudness (LUFS, 10 buckets), bandwidth f_max (Hz, 10 buckets), **speaking rate (UTF-8 bytes per second, 30 buckets)**; each row has an "unknown" index; bucket edges in `params.json` (`condition_edges`) | | Decoder | causal multi-resolution iSTFT head: `full_mr` (default) or `keep2_plain` (pruned, about 3x faster decode) | | Precision | bf16 weights (`model.pth`); decoder heads run in fp32 | ![ZAC 1 audio codec](assets/arch_zac1_dark.png) *ZAC 1 (Zyphra Audio Codec 1).* ## Evaluations Full results and the ZTTS2 capability index are in the [blog post](https://www.zyphra.com/our-work/zonos3-mini#evaluation). Quality against speed on one H100 80GB. Quality combines macro speaker similarity and macro WER over the 55 language subsets of [ZTTS2-Eval](https://zyphra.github.io/ZTTS2-Eval/) (benchmark version 2: FLEURS-R read speech in 35 languages and VoxBlink2 in-the-wild recordings in 20 languages) as ½ z(similarity) − ½ z(WER) across the systems shown; ZONOS3-Mini is measured with the speaker-embedding prompt. Left: median time to first audio with 8 concurrent requests (80 ms for ZONOS3-Mini). Right: peak throughput at each model's best concurrency (457 seconds of audio per second for ZONOS3-Mini). ![ZONOS3-Mini quality versus time to first audio and throughput](assets/eval_pareto.png) ## Citation If you find this model useful in an academic context, please cite the technical report: ```bibtex @misc{zyphra2026zonos3mini, title = {{ZONOS3-Mini Technical Report}}, author = {Gabriel Clark and Sofian Mejjoute and George Close and Beren Millidge}, year = {2026}, eprint = {2611.16525}, archivePrefix = {arXiv}, primaryClass = {cs.SD}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16525}, } ```

# ZONOS3-Mini for 🤗 Transformers

[ZONOS3-Mini](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini) is Zyphra's compact text-to-speech model supporting
43 languages, with about 100 million active parameters per token (800 million total in the backbone). This repo
packages it for plain `transformers` (remote code, `trust_remote_code=True`): the language model, the causal
multi-resolution iSTFT codec decoder (`keep2_plain`) and the MECT-B2 speaker encoder in one checkpoint, with the
SuperBPE tokenizer and the 27 release voices. It synthesizes 44.1 kHz mono speech on CPU or GPU with nothing but
`torch` and `transformers`.

Model details, samples and evaluations: the [blog post](https://www.zyphra.com/our-work/zonos3-mini) and
[technical report](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16525). The native runtimes (CUDA, MLX, ggml, WebGPU) and the full HTTP API
live in the [ZONOS3-Mini repository](https://github.com/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini). Try the
[browser studio](https://zyphra.com/zonos3-mini/localplayground#cast), its
[Lite voice-cloning interface](https://zyphra.com/zonos3-mini/localplayground/lite), or
[Zyphra Cloud](https://cloud.zyphra.com/models/zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini).

## Languages

The same 43 languages as the [main model](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini), with the native runtimes'
request codes (English has two locales):

| Region | Languages (`language` code) |
|---|---|
| Western and Southern Europe | English (`en_us`, `en_gb`), French (`fr_fr`), Spanish (`es`), German (`de`), Italian (`it`), Portuguese (`pt_br`), Dutch (`nl`), Greek (`el`) |
| Northern Europe | Swedish (`sv`), Danish (`da`), Norwegian (`no`), Finnish (`fi`) |
| Central and Eastern Europe | Polish (`pl`), Czech (`cs`), Slovak (`sk`), Hungarian (`hu`), Romanian (`ro`), Bulgarian (`bg`), Russian (`ru`), Ukrainian (`uk`) |
| Middle East and Caucasus | Turkish (`tr`), Arabic (`ar`), Hebrew (`he`), Georgian (`ka`) |
| East Asia | Mandarin Chinese (`cmn`), Japanese (`ja`), Korean (`ko`) |
| Southeast Asia | Vietnamese (`vi`), Indonesian (`id`), Malay (`ms`), Thai (`th`), Tagalog (`tl`) |
| South Asia | Hindi (`hi`), Bengali (`bn`), Tamil (`ta`), Telugu (`te`), Marathi (`mr`), Gujarati (`gu`), Kannada (`kn`), Malayalam (`ml`), Punjabi (`pa`), Odia (`or`), Urdu (`ur`) |

Text normalization uses NeMo grammars via `zyphra_textnorm` for English, Mandarin, Japanese, Korean, German,
Spanish, French, Italian and Portuguese. Other languages pass through as written, with line breaks collapsed;
they do not require the optional normalizer. `language` selects normalization, not a language token in the prompt.

## Usage

```bash
pip install "transformers>=4.57" torch soundfile
pip install zyphra-textnorm   # optional, recommended: reads numbers, dates, currencies and units aloud
```

```python
import soundfile as sf
import torch
from transformers import AutoModel

model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini-hf", trust_remote_code=True)
model = model.to("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")

out = model.generate("Hello! This is ZONOS3-Mini running in transformers.", voice="Savannah", seed=0)
sf.write("hello.wav", out.waveform.numpy(), out.sampling_rate)
```

`AutoModelForTextToWaveform` loads the same class. The checkpoint's LM is bfloat16 (the release dtype): transformers
5 loads it as stored, transformers 4.x in float32 unless you pass `dtype=torch.bfloat16`. The codec decoder and the
speaker encoder always stay in float32. `dtype=torch.float32` gives the reference numerics on CPU.

### Voices

Pick one voice source per call:

| Argument | Conditioning |
|---|---|
| `voice="Savannah"` | a release voice (below): its reference codes, or its speaker embedding with `speaker_mode="embedding"` |
| `speaker_audio=wav, speaker_sample_rate=sr` | a clip ([samples] or [channels, samples], any rate) through the speaker encoder |
| `speaker_embedding=emb` | a 192-d speaker embedding (`model.embed_speaker(wav, sr)` computes one) |
| `speaker_reference_codes=codes` | precomputed codec codes [frames, 10] of a clip (at most 60 s used) |

`speaker_mode` defaults to `"reference"` for voices and codes and to `"embedding"` for clips and embeddings.
`speaker_cfg_scale` (default 1.0) above 1 strengthens the voice through classifier-free guidance (a second LM pass
per step). Encoding a raw clip into codec codes needs the codec encoder of the native runtimes; here clips clone
through the speaker embedding.

```python
import soundfile as sf

wav, sr = sf.read("my_voice.wav", dtype="float32", always_2d=True)
out = model.generate("Cloned from a clip.", speaker_audio=wav.T, speaker_sample_rate=sr, seed=1)

emb = model.embed_speaker(wav.T, sr)  # reuse it across calls
out = model.generate("Same voice, from its embedding.", speaker_embedding=emb, seed=1)
```

### Options

| Argument | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `language` | `"en_us"` | a request code from [Languages](#languages); case-insensitive, accepts `-` for `_` |
| `text_normalization` | `True` | `zyphra_textnorm` when installed (otherwise a one-time warning and line breaks collapsed only) |
| `condition_values` | unknown | `{"loudness": LUFS, "fmax": Hz, "speaking_rate": UTF-8 bytes per second}` (or a list of 3) |
| `condition_buckets` | unknown | the same as bucket ids (loudness / fmax 0..9, speaking rate 0..29) |
| `temperature`, `topk`, `top_p`, `min_p` | 0.75, 80, 0.69, 0.0 | sampling |
| `repetition_penalty`, `repetition_window`, `repetition_codebooks` | 2.4, 96, 6 | repetition penalty |
| `silence_prefill_frames` | 3 | codec silence frames opening the take (0..30) |
| `decode_context`, `decode_context_frames` | `False`, 30 | decode the reference tail as left context (reference mode) |
| `max_new_frames` | context left | frame budget (15 frames per second) |
| `seed` | random | the take's seed (returned in `out.seed`) |
| `headroom_db`, `fade_out_ms` | 3.0, 0.0 | output gain (then a soft limiter at -1 dBFS) and fade-out |

`generate` returns `waveform` (float32 [samples]), `sampling_rate` (44100), `seed` and `codes` (the decoded codec
frames [frames, 10]). `model.decode_codes(codes)` turns codes into audio; `model(input_ids=rows, cache=cache)` runs one
LM step over prompt rows [rows, 11] for custom decoding loops.

## Architecture

| Component | ZONOS3-Mini |
|---|---|
| Backbone | 11 layers, dimension 1,024; latent MoE with 64 experts, top-2 routing from layer 1 |
| Sequence mixer | 9 Gated DeltaNet layers + 2 global attention layers, Full AttnRes; context 32,768 positions |
| Text | SuperBPE, 8,192 entries + 4 special tokens |
| Audio tokens | 15 Hz; 10 codebooks of 4,096 entries (1 semantic + 9 acoustic); hop 2,940 samples at 44.1 kHz |
| Speaker prompt | codec reference prefix (up to 60 s) or a 192-d MECT-B2 embedding |
| Decoder | bundled `keep2_plain` causal multi-resolution iSTFT head; the native release also offers `full_mr` (its default) |

## Notes

- The backbone configuration, tokenizer and 27 release voices match
  [upstream revision `727302c1`](https://huggingface.co/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/tree/727302c1cb61bee229a649d859ebb3e517da1a41).
  Request languages follow the native
  [language registry](https://github.com/Zyphra/ZONOS3-Mini/blob/4df58c814db9163f4bf3f717e9bca49e334a1827/model/src/zonos3/registries/languages.json).
- The prompt layout, sampler, EOS handling, codec and speaker encoder follow the reference implementation of the
  ZONOS3-Mini repository. The LM is vectorized (chunked gated-delta rule, grouped experts), so its logits match the
  reference within float tolerance and long sampled takes may drift from it.
- Not included: speech editing, steering controls and accents, LACI, phoneme input, tag CFG, streaming decode and the
  codec encoder. The native runtimes serve them.
- The `text-to-speech` pipeline is not supported: it tokenizes before the model sees the text, which skips the text
  normalization. Call `generate` with the raw text.

OmniVoice is a massively multilingual zero-shot text-to-speech (TTS) model supporting over 600 languages. Built on a novel diffusion language model-style architecture, it delivers high-quality speech with superior inference speed, supporting voice cloning and voice design. - **Paper:** [OmniVoice: Towards Omnilingual Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech with Diffusion Language Models](https://huggingface.co/papers/2604.00688) - **Repository:** [GitHub](https://github.com/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) - **Demo:** [Hugging Face Space](https://huggingface.co/spaces/k2-fsa/OmniVoice) - **Colab:** [Google Colab Notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/k2-fsa/OmniVoice/blob/master/docs/OmniVoice.ipynb) ## Key Features - **600+ Languages Supported**: The broadest language coverage among zero-shot TTS models. - **Voice Cloning**: State-of-the-art voice cloning quality from a short reference audio. - **Voice Design**: Control voices via assigned speaker attributes (gender, age, pitch, dialect/accent, whisper, etc.). - **Fine-grained Control**: Non-verbal symbols (e.g., `[laughter]`) and pronunciation correction via pinyin or phonemes. - **Fast Inference**: RTF as low as 0.025 (40x faster than real-time). - **Diffusion Language Model-style Architecture**: A clean, streamlined, and scalable design that delivers both quality and speed. ## Usage To get started, install the `omnivoice` library: > We recommend using a fresh virtual environment (e.g., `conda`, `venv`, etc.) to avoid conflicts. **Step 1**: Install PyTorch

# Sudanese Chatterbox v0.1 (ft2)

A text-to-speech model for **Sudanese Arabic** that clones a voice from a short reference clip. It is
[lahgtna-chatterbox-v1](https://huggingface.co/oddadmix/lahgtna-chatterbox-v1) (Chatterbox Multilingual,
fine-tuned for Arabic dialects), fine-tuned again on 4.7 hours of openly licensed Sudanese speech. MIT licence:
free for research and commercial use.

## What fine-tuning changed
Tested on 50 Sudanese sentences in 4 real Sudanese voices that were never in training (full method:
[results/README.md](https://github.com/MontaserAlajamy/sudanese-arabic-tts/blob/main/results/README.md) in the [project repository](https://github.com/MontaserAlajamy/sudanese-arabic-tts)).

| | base (lahgtna-chatterbox) | **this model** | real Sudanese speech |
|---|---|---|---|
| Whisper CER, capped at 1 per clip ↓ | 0.474 | **0.264** | 0.126 |
| clips flagged "wrong or missing word" by a native listener | 12 of 14 | **1 of 13** | – |
| native listener: "Sudanese?" (1-5) | 3.50 | **3.62** | – |
| native listener: "natural?" (1-5) | 3.21 | **3.46** | – |
| ق said as [g] where the dialect wants it | 5 of 5 | 5 of 5 | – |

In the same blind round the best commercial service scored 4.33 / 4.42, so a clear gap remains.

## Samples
All 12 listening sentences of the benchmark, not hand-picked, each with the native listener's blind rating
(Sudanese / natural, 1-5). Voices are cloned from speakers of the Omnilingual ASR corpus (CC-BY-4.0).

| 2 | هسع ببني المشهد تلاتي الأبعاد أول: الأوضة، وكل زول في محلو. | spk08 | 2 / 2 | [o07.mp3](samples/o07.mp3) |

| 6 | شنو الحاصل؟ الناس دي ماشة وين بالحيل كدا؟ | spk08 | 4 / 4 | [d06.mp3](samples/d06.mp3) |

## Use
Needs the lahgtna-chatterbox code (pinned commit below) and a 6-10 s reference clip of the voice, used with the
speaker's consent.
```bash
git clone https://github.com/Oddadmix/lahgtna-chatterbox && cd lahgtna-chatterbox
git checkout 433cb74200b55457bffa8ee6965a02ecab546a1c && pip install -e .
# its alignment analyzer needs attention maps: in src/chatterbox/models/t3/llama_configs.py
# change attn_implementation="sdpa" to "eager"
```
```python
import torch, soundfile as sf
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from safetensors.torch import load_file
from chatterbox.mtl_tts import ChatterboxMultilingualTTS

model = ChatterboxMultilingualTTS.from_pretrained(device="cuda")
t3 = hf_hub_download("MuntasirElagami/sudanese-chatterbox", "t3_mtl23ls_v2.safetensors")
model.t3.load_state_dict(load_file(t3, device="cuda"))
model.t3.eval()
wav = model.generate("يا زول، إنت جيت متين من الخرطوم؟", language_id="sd", audio_prompt_path="reference.wav",
                     exaggeration=0.5, temperature=0.8, cfg_weight=0.5)
sf.write("out.wav", wav.squeeze().cpu().numpy(), model.sr)
```
`language_id="sd"` is lahgtna's Sudanese slot. Plain Arabic text works best; tashkeel is not needed.

## Training
- Data: [sudanese-arabic-speech](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MuntasirElagami/sudanese-arabic-speech), train split
  (8 speakers), `tts_ready` clips only: 1,956 clips, 4.72 h. Derived from the Omnilingual ASR Corpus (`apd_Arab`),
  Omnilingual ASR Team, Meta FAIR (2025), CC-BY-4.0.
- Only the T3 (text-to-speech-token) model is trained; the speech decoder and voice encoder are Chatterbox's own.
- 3 epochs, 735 optimizer steps, batch 2 × gradient accumulation 4, lr 2e-5, warmup 30; one free Kaggle T4,
  65 minutes. Training loss 6.4 → 4.1. Code: `jobs/train_chatterbox_job.py`, `scripts/train.py`.

## Limits
- Speaks fast: about 9.4 letters per second against 8.5 for the real speakers, and it still drops a word now and then.
- Evaluated by one native listener on 12 sentences; the gain over the base model is clear on word accuracy and
  small on accent.
- Trained on spontaneous speech of 8 adults; not tested on long passages, children's voices or other Sudanese
  regional accents.

## Responsible use
Clone only a voice whose owner has agreed. Do not use the model to impersonate anyone or to make speech that
someone did not say look real. Note: the lahgtna-chatterbox code at this commit does not watermark its output
(the Perth watermark call is commented out); if you publish generated speech, add it back:
`wav = model.watermarker.apply_watermark(wav, sample_rate=model.sr)` on the NumPy waveform.

MIT, like Chatterbox (Resemble AI) and lahgtna-chatterbox (oddadmix). Training audio: Omnilingual ASR Team,
Meta FAIR (2025), CC-BY-4.0.
